lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Mastery check: shared-space agreements and boundaries

objective: Learners draft one real, specific shared-space agreement (such as about a common area, a chore split, or quiet hours) and actually propose it to their real household, with a trusted adult confirming afterward that the conversation took place.
scenario: The learner identifies one real point of friction or unclear expectation in a shared space in their real household, drafts a specific written agreement addressing it, and proposes the agreement out loud to the household members it affects. A trusted adult confirms the conversation happened.
safetyNotes: The learner proposes the agreement as a conversation, not a written contract requiring signatures; no household member is required to agree on the spot.

Completing this task sheet never certifies the proposal by itself; a guardian confirmation that the conversation happened is required before the task counts as complete, exactly as this course's own safety policy states.

simulationAlternative.description: If proposing the agreement to the full household is not possible during the lesson window, the learner instead writes the complete agreement and then role-plays the full proposal conversation with a trusted adult, including the adult responding with at least one realistic objection or question for the learner to address.

materials: access to the real household members the agreement affects, or a trusted adult for the role-played version

tasks.directions: Identify one real point of friction or unclear expectation in a shared space in your household.

prompts.text: Describe the specific shared space (for example, a bathroom, kitchen, living room, or laundry area) and the specific problem or unclear expectation around it.

tasks.directions: Draft your agreement with three specific parts: what the expectation is, who it applies to, and what happens if it isn't followed.

prompts.text: My agreement names the specific shared space and the specific expectation, not a vague goal like 'be more considerate.'
My agreement names exactly who it applies to.
My agreement states a specific, reasonable next step if the expectation isn't met.

tasks.directions: Propose your agreement out loud to the household members it affects, listen to their response, and note what happened.

prompts.text: What was the outcome of proposing your agreement?
choices: Accepted with changes we agreed on together
Not yet resolved, more discussion needed

prompts.text: Write down one specific thing a household member said in response, whether it was agreement, a question, or pushback.
What is one thing you would say differently if you proposed this agreement again, based on how the actual conversation went?

remediation: If a learner's agreement states only a vague goal ('everyone should help more') without naming the specific space, specific expectation, and specific people it applies to, reteach by having them rewrite it as a single sentence following the exact frame 'In [space], [person or people] will [specific action] by [specific time or trigger]' before proposing it.
extension: Have the learner draft a second agreement for a different shared space and identify which of the two agreements is more likely to actually get followed, explaining why in terms of how specific and enforceable each one is.
